vignette:
Maya Ortiz, a 44-year-old chaplain, came to treatment carrying a trauma history that still felt painfully immediate to her. Years earlier, while she was serving in a city hospital and later supporting a community vigil for victims of terrorism, a bomb had detonated nearby. She had been speaking quietly with a grieving family when the blast shattered glass, dropped people to the ground, and turned the scene into chaos in a matter of seconds. In the days and weeks after, every sudden noise or startled face seemed to tell Maya the same thing with quiet certainty: this could happen again, and nowhere she stood was truly safe. Those moments did not just unsettle her; they immediately became proof, in her mind, that the world had changed into a place she could not rely on. When a tray slammed in the hospital cafeteria or a burst of laughter rose in a hallway, Maya would leave her food untouched and step out before she could feel cornered, telling herself that it was safer to keep moving than to stay where her body could be caught off guard. The same sounds drove her to count under her breath and repeat phrases in private, as if those small routines might hold danger at bay. What stayed with Maya was not only the terror itself but the sense that the ordinary world had been abruptly, cruelly violated. In the months afterward, she found that anything that hinted at joy, celebration, or ease could unsettle her; a birthday song in the cafeteria, laughter in a hallway, even a colleague’s casual bright mood could leave her uneasy and strangely ashamed, as if positive emotion belonged to a world that had not proved trustworthy. Those moments fed her belief that the world was dangerous and that institutions and people who should have protected her had let her down. With each of those cues, the conclusion came quickly: if ordinary pleasure could be shattered so suddenly, then nowhere was truly reliable, and she began to notice new signs of risk everywhere she went. Each time she heard celebration spilling from the cafeteria or saw a uniform at a doorway, the thought arrived with it that life would never be predictable again and that she had to stay guarded or be caught unprepared. The cues did not just alarm her; they pressed her into the same bleak certainty about the world, and that certainty was what made her scan for exits, avoid staff meetings, and keep herself away from situations where something might happen without warning. A laughing group in the corridor, a bright mood in a coworker, or the sound of celebration in the hospital cafeteria all seemed to confirm that danger could break through at any moment. She began avoiding full meals and restricting food when she felt flooded, telling herself that if she kept herself light and controlled she might be less vulnerable to whatever came next. She also started silently repeating phrases and counting in her head, trying to prevent bad things from happening again, a private ritual that made sense to her as a desperate way of restoring order in a life that had been split open.

As time passed, Maya’s sense of herself darkened alongside her view of the world. She had once imagined herself as steady in crisis, but now she saw her reactions—her fear, her vigilance, her need to arrange every detail—as proof that she was a lousy coper. That belief kept pulling her back to the bombing in her mind, as if she needed to rehearse the scene again and again to locate where she had failed. The memory became more vivid whenever she judged herself this way, returning with the same metallic taste, ringing ears, and smoke that made it feel less like remembering than being dropped back into it. That belief made her scan herself and her surroundings differently, so that the same small noise or abrupt movement that she might once have brushed off now snagged her attention and felt like evidence that she could not trust her own judgment. The more she decided she was not coping well, the more she treated ordinary moments as potential warnings. That appraisal made it harder for her to trust her own judgment, and when she recalled the bombing, the memory did not arrive like a normal recollection. The conviction that she was a lousy coper sent her back to the scene over and over, as if she had to find the moment she failed and prove to herself that she should have been stronger. Each return made it harder to step into ordinary situations without bracing for disaster, because the memory itself seemed to confirm that she was not built to handle what came. Because she was already convinced that disaster was always close, a loud tray dropped in the hospital cafeteria or a uniformed officer at a doorway could snag her attention at once and take on the force of a warning. The thought that she could not trust herself to read danger correctly meant that even a laugh in the corridor or a bright, celebratory mood around her felt suspicious, as if it were hiding the next blow. It came back with full sensory force: the metallic taste of dust, the ringing in her ears, the smell of smoke, the sight of blood on clothing, all of it feeling completely real across her senses at once. The fragments would come in the wrong order, leaving her unable to tell whether she heard the blast before seeing people fall or whether the shouting began first. When the memory hit like that, Maya would avoid the places and routines that seemed most likely to call it up again — meals in the hospital cafeteria, public celebrations, even lingering near uniforms — because she did not trust herself to stay steady if the scene returned while she was there. She kept her rituals going for the same reason, counting and repeating phrases until the images dulled enough for her to keep functioning. Because the memory felt more vivid than ordinary life, it would be set off by the kinds of things she had come to fear in daily life: an unexpected bang in the street outside her apartment, a loud tray dropped in the hospital cafeteria where she sometimes volunteered, or the sight of a uniformed officer at the entrance to a building. Each cue pushed her back into the same conviction that disaster could strike without warning and that she would be left unprotected again. She became especially unsettled by people misbehaving or acting arrogantly; a brusque tone at work or someone ignoring a line in public could stir the old sense that order could collapse in an instant. The sense of danger itself had become proof to her that life had changed beyond repair, and she began to accept the thought that she was now someone who had to live on guard. Feeling that threat so persistently, she came to believe not only that the world was unsafe, but that this frightened vigilance was simply who she was now.

Those experiences kept feeding her habits. Maya began choosing seats with great care wherever she went, favoring corners, backs to walls, and clear views of exits. At the hospital, in the church basement, and even in small neighborhood cafés, she scanned other people closely for signs that they might harm her, reading posture, hands, and faces with the intensity of someone trying to stay alive. Loud or unexpected sounds kept her on high alert, and she would stiffen before she could think. At the same time, her repeated mental rituals and food restriction offered a temporary illusion of control, but they also kept her body in a state of tension that made every sound and movement feel more dangerous. Because she never stayed long enough in those moments for anything to settle, her body never got the evidence that the danger had passed. The counting, the restriction, and the careful control made the threat feel as if it were still active, exactly as real as it had been on the day of the bombing. The more she tried to manage risk through these routines, the more she felt exposed to it. Her wariness made it hard to relax even in spaces that should have felt familiar, and her growing distrust of authority figures and uniforms complicated the work that had once given her meaning. She started avoiding staff meetings where police liaisons or emergency personnel were present, and she would find excuses not to linger after services if a uniformed visitor arrived.

By the time she sought help, Maya was exhausted by the way the bombing still governed her days. She was no longer only remembering what happened; she was living as though danger might return at any moment, and every vivid flash of the event seemed to confirm that her fear was justified. What finally brought her in was realizing that she had begun shrinking her life around these fears—eating less, watching everyone, choosing her seats like a survivor planning an escape route—and that even her work as a chaplain was being narrowed by the conviction that the world, and the people who were supposed to safeguard it, could not be trusted. She said she wanted to stop feeling as if the blast were still happening in her body, and she was most afraid that if she could not find a way to loosen her grip on control, she would remain trapped in a life organized entirely around preventing the next catastrophe.

  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Maya Ortiz, a 44-year-old chaplain, came to treatment carrying a trauma history that still felt painfully immediate to her. Years earlier, while she was serving in a city hospital and later supporting a community vigil for victims of terrorism, a bomb had detonated nearby. She had been speaking quietly with a grieving family when the blast shattered glass, dropped people to the ground, and turned the scene into chaos in a matter of seconds. In the days and weeks after, every sudden noise or startled face seemed to tell Maya the same thing with quiet certainty: this could happen again, and nowhere she stood was truly safe. Those moments did not just unsettle her; they immediately became proof, in her mind, that the world had changed into a place she could not rely on. When a tray slammed in the hospital cafeteria or a burst of laughter rose in a hallway, Maya would leave her food untouched and step out before she could feel cornered, telling herself that it was safer to keep moving than to stay where her body could be caught off guard. The same sounds drove her to count under her breath and repeat phrases in private, as if those small routines might hold danger at bay. What stayed with Maya was not only the terror itself but the sense that the ordinary world had been abruptly, cruelly violated. In the months afterward, she found that anything that hinted at joy, celebration, or ease could unsettle her; a birthday song in the cafeteria, laughter in a hallway, even a colleague’s casual bright mood could leave her uneasy and strangely ashamed, as if positive emotion belonged to a world that had not proved trustworthy. Those moments fed her belief that the world was dangerous and that institutions and people who should have protected her had let her down. With each of those cues, the conclusion came quickly: if ordinary pleasure could be shattered so suddenly, then nowhere was truly reliable, and she began to notice new signs of risk everywhere she went. Each time she heard celebration spilling from the cafeteria or saw a uniform at a doorway, the thought arrived with it that life would never be predictable again and that she had to stay guarded or be caught unprepared. The cues did not just alarm her; they pressed her into the same bleak certainty about the world, and that certainty was what made her scan for exits, avoid staff meetings, and keep herself away from situations where something might happen without warning. A laughing group in the corridor, a bright mood in a coworker, or the sound of celebration in the hospital cafeteria all seemed to confirm that danger could break through at any moment. She began avoiding full meals and restricting food when she felt flooded, telling herself that if she kept herself light and controlled she might be less vulnerable to whatever came next. She also started silently repeating phrases and counting in her head, trying to prevent bad things from happening again, a private ritual that made sense to her as a desperate way of restoring order in a life that had been split open.

As time passed, Maya’s sense of herself darkened alongside her view of the world. She had once imagined herself as steady in crisis, but now she saw her reactions—her fear, her vigilance, her need to arrange every detail—as proof that she was a lousy coper. That belief kept pulling her back to the bombing in her mind, as if she needed to rehearse the scene again and again to locate where she had failed. The memory became more vivid whenever she judged herself this way, returning with the same metallic taste, ringing ears, and smoke that made it feel less like remembering than being dropped back into it. That belief made her scan herself and her surroundings differently, so that the same small noise or abrupt movement that she might once have brushed off now snagged her attention and felt like evidence that she could not trust her own judgment. The more she decided she was not coping well, the more she treated ordinary moments as potential warnings. That appraisal made it harder for her to trust her own judgment, and when she recalled the bombing, the memory did not arrive like a normal recollection. The conviction that she was a lousy coper sent her back to the scene over and over, as if she had to find the moment she failed and prove to herself that she should have been stronger. Each return made it harder to step into ordinary situations without bracing for disaster, because the memory itself seemed to confirm that she was not built to handle what came. Because she was already convinced that disaster was always close, a loud tray dropped in the hospital cafeteria or a uniformed officer at a doorway could snag her attention at once and take on the force of a warning. The thought that she could not trust herself to read danger correctly meant that even a laugh in the corridor or a bright, celebratory mood around her felt suspicious, as if it were hiding the next blow. It came back with full sensory force: the metallic taste of dust, the ringing in her ears, the smell of smoke, the sight of blood on clothing, all of it feeling completely real across her senses at once. The fragments would come in the wrong order, leaving her unable to tell whether she heard the blast before seeing people fall or whether the shouting began first. When the memory hit like that, Maya would avoid the places and routines that seemed most likely to call it up again — meals in the hospital cafeteria, public celebrations, even lingering near uniforms — because she did not trust herself to stay steady if the scene returned while she was there. She kept her rituals going for the same reason, counting and repeating phrases until the images dulled enough for her to keep functioning. Because the memory felt more vivid than ordinary life, it would be set off by the kinds of things she had come to fear in daily life: an unexpected bang in the street outside her apartment, a loud tray dropped in the hospital cafeteria where she sometimes volunteered, or the sight of a uniformed officer at the entrance to a building. Each cue pushed her back into the same conviction that disaster could strike without warning and that she would be left unprotected again. She became especially unsettled by people misbehaving or acting arrogantly; a brusque tone at work or someone ignoring a line in public could stir the old sense that order could collapse in an instant. The sense of danger itself had become proof to her that life had changed beyond repair, and she began to accept the thought that she was now someone who had to live on guard. Feeling that threat so persistently, she came to believe not only that the world was unsafe, but that this frightened vigilance was simply who she was now.

Those experiences kept feeding her habits. Maya began choosing seats with great care wherever she went, favoring corners, backs to walls, and clear views of exits. At the hospital, in the church basement, and even in small neighborhood cafés, she scanned other people closely for signs that they might harm her, reading posture, hands, and faces with the intensity of someone trying to stay alive. Loud or unexpected sounds kept her on high alert, and she would stiffen before she could think. At the same time, her repeated mental rituals and food restriction offered a temporary illusion of control, but they also kept her body in a state of tension that made every sound and movement feel more dangerous. Because she never stayed long enough in those moments for anything to settle, her body never got the evidence that the danger had passed. The counting, the restriction, and the careful control made the threat feel as if it were still active, exactly as real as it had been on the day of the bombing. The more she tried to manage risk through these routines, the more she felt exposed to it. Her wariness made it hard to relax even in spaces that should have felt familiar, and her growing distrust of authority figures and uniforms complicated the work that had once given her meaning. She started avoiding staff meetings where police liaisons or emergency personnel were present, and she would find excuses not to linger after services if a uniformed visitor arrived.

By the time she sought help, Maya was exhausted by the way the bombing still governed her days. She was no longer only remembering what happened; she was living as though danger might return at any moment, and every vivid flash of the event seemed to confirm that her fear was justified. What finally brought her in was realizing that she had begun shrinking her life around these fears—eating less, watching everyone, choosing her seats like a survivor planning an escape route—and that even her work as a chaplain was being narrowed by the conviction that the world, and the people who were supposed to safeguard it, could not be trusted. She said she wanted to stop feeling as if the blast were still happening in her body, and she was most afraid that if she could not find a way to loosen her grip on control, she would remain trapped in a life organized entirely around preventing the next catastrophe.
